The row now reads 'For an AR(1) series with \(\phi \gt 0\), the iid bootstrap understates the standard error of the mean by \(\sqrt{(1+\phi)/(1-\phi)}\)', grade T, 'Derived in section 3'. Re-derived: for x_t = phi x_{t-1} + e_t, |phi| < 1, gamma(h) = sigma^2 phi^|h|/(1 - phi^2), so sum_h gamma(h) = sigma^2/(1-phi)^2 and the ratio of the long-run to the iid variance gamma(0) is (1+phi)/(1-phi) (section 3 displays exactly this chain). The iid bootstrap variance of the mean is gamma-hat(0)/T, so true SE / iid SE = sqrt((1+phi)/(1-phi)): 1.732 at phi = 0.5 (ratio 3), 1.5275 at 0.4, exactly 1 at phi = 0 (no understatement, hence the strict inequality is right), and 0.577 at phi = -0.5 (ratio 1/3), where the iid value is 1.73 times too large. For phi > 0 the ratio exceeds 1 because 1 + phi > 1 - phi, so 'understates' holds for every phi in (0, 1): the row is now exactly true in its stated domain. The quoted factor is the large-T limit that section 3 displays (T Var(x-bar) -> ...); at T = 500 and phi = 0.5 the exact finite-sample factor is sqrt(2.992) = 1.730 against 1.732 (2.992 = 3 - 1/125, the T Var(d-bar) printed by Problem E4), so the table is right as an asymptotic statement and consistent with the page's own T = 500 numbers. Every other place on the page that says 'understates' is conditioned: section 3 text at phi = 0.5, the figure caption 'With positive autocorrelation (phi > 0)', M3 (phi in {0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.6}), quiz item 5 (phi = 0.5), and Remark 3.5 ('with phi gt 0'); a grep of L03, L04, index.html and cards.json for 'understate' finds no other unqualified AR(1) claim. Steps: (1) conditional on the data, Var(sum_t eps_t d_t | d) = sum_t d_t^2 for independent signs with mean 0 and variance 1, so T^(-1) sum_t d_t^2 is the conditional variance and (H1) gives gamma(0). (5) Slutsky's lemma (|S_T| has a continuous limit law at the cut-off, and the cut-off converges in probability) gives P(|S_T| > cut-off) -> 2(1 - Phi(1.96 sqrt(gamma(0)/sigma2_LR))) = 2(1 - Phi(1.96 sqrt((1-phi)/(1+phi)))). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L03.html Lemma 2.3 (line 102) and its proof; card S7-c217
rows.evidence: unchanged since 5246c33 (git diff checked); round-14 evidence: Re-derived. (a) p_(k) <= kq/m iff at least k p-values are <= kq/m: if p_(k) <= kq/m then p_(1..k) are all <= kq/m, so N(k) >= k; if N(k) >= k then the k-th smallest is <= kq/m. Hence R = max{k : N(k) >= k}. (b) If R >= 1, a rejected H_i has p_i <= p_(R) <= Rq/m. Conversely, if p_i <= Rq/m but p_i = p_(j) with j > R, then p_(j) <= Rq/m <= jq/m, so N(j) >= j, contradicting the maximality of R; the zero case is handled (N(1) >= 1 forces R >= 1). (c) Raising a p-value can only lower each N(k), so the largest k with N(k) >= k cannot increase. Numerical spot check (scratch py/spotchecks_r12.py): for 2,000 random p-vectors (m = 10, q = 0.05, mixed scales) the BH rejection set equals {i : p_i <= R q/m} with R = max{k : N(k) >= k} (0 violations), and R does not increase when one randomly chosen p-value is raised (0 violations). Ties: the proof uses the k-th smallest p-value, so ties do not change the count.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L03.html Proposition 5.3 (line 281) and its proof; card S7-c218
rows.evidence: unchanged since 5246c33 (git diff checked); round-14 evidence: Re-derived for rho in [0,1). Given z_i = t, the joint Gaussian (W, z_i) gives W | z_i = t ~ N(sqrt(rho)(t - mu_i), 1 - rho), stochastically increasing in t for rho >= 0 (the constant case rho = 0 is trivially monotone). The other coordinates are z_j = sqrt(rho) W + sqrt(1-rho) eps_j + mu_j with eps_j independent of (W, z_i), so P(z in D' | z_i = t) = E[g(W) | z_i = t], g non-increasing for a decreasing D' (translating all z_j by a common amount). Hence t -> P(z in D' | z_i = t) is non-increasing, which is PRDS (Definition 5.1) on every subset. Numerical spot check (scratch py/spotchecks_r12.py, Monte Carlo 600,000 draws, rho = 0.5, m = 3, D = {p_2 >= 1/2, p_3 >= 1/2}, an increasing set in p-space): P(D | z_1 near t) falls from 0.556 at t = -1 to 0.033 at t = 2 (non-increasing in t), and P(D | p_1 near u) rises from 0.054 at u = 0.05 to 0.708 at u = 0.95 (non-decreasing in u): the PRDS inequality holds in the numerical check. (An earlier attempt used the z-increasing set {z_2 > 0, z_3 > 0}; that set is not an increasing set of p-values, so it was discarded.)

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L04.html line 365 (section 6, the T span: 'Step 2 of Definition 4.1 subtracts each strategy's own sample mean ... never more')
rows.evidence: unchanged since 5246c33 (git diff checked); round-14 evidence: Re-derived from Definition 4.1 (L04.html lines 268–275: V_K = max_k sqrt(T) dbar_k; V*_{K,j} = max_k sqrt(T)(dbar*_{k,j} - dbar_k) with one index sequence per draw shared by all strategies; p-hat = mean_j 1{V*_{K,j} >= V_K}). (a) Adding any strategy adds one term to each maximum: V*_{K+1,j} = max(V*_{K,j}, term_j) >= V*_{K,j} for every draw j. (b) If its statistic s = sqrt(T) dbar_{K+1} is not the largest (s <= V_K), then V_{K+1} = V_K. (c) Hence with the same draws p-hat can only rise, and rejection at alpha (p-hat <= alpha) can only be lost. Numerical check of (a)–(c) with the Definition 4.1 procedure, seed 20261020, 300 trials, T = 120, B = 400, K from 2 to 7 (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify22h-L03-L04/derive/rc_pathwise_check.py, output /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify22h-L03-L04/derive/rc_pathwise_check.out): non-largest additions 210: V_K unchanged in 210 of 210; V*_(K+1,j) >= V*_(K,j) for every draw in all 300 trials (0 violations); p-hat fell in 0 of 210. Control (d): when the added statistic is the largest, p-hat fell in 74 of 90 trials, so the claim needs the 'not the largest' condition. The span's clause 'such a poor alternative can make the Reality Check reject less often, never more' refers, through 'such', to a strategy whose statistic is not the largest; read pathwise (same data and draws) it is exactly (a)–(c). The vocabulary is now the lesson's 'centred at zero' (Definition 4.1 step 2 subtracts the sample mean; Theorem 3.2(d) gives zero bootstrap mean). No citation is needed (proved on the page). rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L04.html line 259 (Remark 3.5): the displayed limit 2(1 - Phi(1.96 sqrt(gamma(0)/sigma2_LR))) and the two numerical values
rows.evidence: Re-derived at 0c8449d. (i) Conditional variance: for independent signs with P(eps = ±1) = 1/2, E[eps_t] = 0, Var(eps_t) = 1, Var(sum_t eps_t d_t | d) = sum_t d_t^2; so Var(T^(-1/2) sum_t eps_t d_t | d) = T^(-1) sum_t d_t^2 -> gamma(0) by (H1). (ii) AR(1) with |phi| < 1, gamma(h) = gamma(0) phi^|h|: sigma2_LR = sum_h gamma(h) = gamma(0)(1 + 2 phi/(1 - phi)) = gamma(0)(1 + phi)/(1 - phi); gamma(0)/sigma2_LR = (1 - phi)/(1 + phi); the factor of the Remark sqrt((1+phi)/(1-phi)) = sigma_LR/sqrt(gamma(0)). Numerically exact (remark35_limits.out, section 1: 1.8571428571 and 3.0000000000 at phi = 0.3 and 0.5). (iii) Given (H1)-(H3), P(|S_T| > c_T) -> P(|N(0, sigma2_LR)| > 1.96 sqrt(gamma(0))) = 2(1 - Phi(1.96 sqrt(gamma(0))/sqrt(sigma2_LR))) = 2(1 - Phi(1.96 sqrt((1-phi)/(1+phi)))). (iv) Values: phi = 0.5: 1.96/sqrt3 = 1.1316065276, limit 0.2577998945 (0.258); phi = 0.3: 1.96 sqrt(7/13) = 1.4382467960, limit 0.1503640418 (0.150). Both match the page to three decimals in either form. The algebra and the limit are right; the sentence naming the 97.5% quantile is the separate defect in L04-math-remark3.5.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L04.html line 259: the hypotheses (H1)-(H3) as printed, and the sentence 'The hypotheses, which this lesson assumes rather than proves, are ...'
rows.evidence: Checked at 0c8449d. The hypotheses are stated and are the ones the derivation uses: (H1) T^(-1) sum_t d_t^2 -> gamma(0) in probability (the conditional variance); (H2) conditional on the data, T^(-1/2) sum_t eps_t d_t -> N(0, gamma(0)) in distribution, in probability, for independent fair signs (the conditional CLT for the sign-flip sum); (H3) T^(-1/2) sum_t d_t -> N(0, sigma2_LR) in distribution (the CLT for the statistic). Nothing else is used: the quantile step and Slutsky's lemma are standard consequences. The hypotheses are not vacuous for the lesson's examples: the Gaussian stationary AR(1) of Lab 1 and Problem E4 (|phi| < 1, rng.standard_normal shocks at L04.html lines 199 and 650, the Lab 1 and Problem E4 code) satisfies a law of large numbers for the squares and a CLT for the mean, and a conditional CLT for Rademacher-weighted sums under the Lindeberg condition max_t d_t^2 / sum_s d_s^2 -> 0 in probability. The Remark does not claim that the lesson proves them, and says so. Advisory (not a fail): 'the series (eps_t d_t) has the same marginal distributions as (d_t)' needs each d_t symmetric about zero. The paragraph states that condition one sentence earlier, and the lesson's AR(1) differentials are Gaussian, so the claim holds in the lesson's setting. If the Remark is generalised, add 'each d_t symmetric about zero' to that sentence. PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L04.html line 259 (the limit) and line 633 (E4 predictions): Monte Carlo spot check of the sign-flip test (derive/signflip_mc.py, signflip_mc.out)
rows.evidence: Run at 0c8449d (18.9 s; seed 20261020; numpy, scipy). Gaussian AR(1), phi = 0.5, T = 2000, 4000 replications, K = 199 random sign patterns per replication, statistic S = |sum d_t|/sqrt(T), reference R_k = |sum eps_kt d_t|/sqrt(T). Output: rejection with the cut-off at the 95% quantile of |R| = 0.2530 (MC SE 0.0069) vs the limit 2(1 - Phi(1.96 sqrt(gamma0/sigma2LR))) = 0.257800 (within 0.7 SE). With the cut-off at the 97.5% quantile of |R| (the literal reading of the Remark's sentence): 0.2040 vs 0.195640. Mean 95% quantile of |R| / sqrt(gamma0) = 1.9401 (theory 1.96); mean 97.5% quantile = 2.2015 (theory 2.2414 for |N(0,1)|; finite K). gamma0 = 1.333333, sigma2LR = 4.000000, ratio 3.000000. The Monte Carlo supports the limit 0.258 and shows that the wording with the 97.5% quantile of |R| would give about 0.20: the defect recorded in L04-math-remark3.5.
